docs.title: Francisco's Dev Journey
docs.text:
Welcome! This is my personal blog where I document the highs, the confusion, and the breakthroughs of becoming a Full-Stack Developer from scratch.

I'm currently enrolled in a full-stack software engineering program, and every week I'll be writing about what I learned, what broke, and what finally clicked. Think of it as a learning journal — raw, honest, and hopefully useful to anyone else on a similar path.

docs.title: What to Expect
docs.text:
Each post follows a simple format:

  • Date — when it happened
  • Title — what the day was about
  • Body — my honest take on it

Posts are organized by week so you can follow along from the beginning or jump to whatever's relevant to you.

docs.title: Week 1 — The Foundation
docs.text:
The first week was all about getting set up and building the mental models that everything else will rest on.

Day Topic Day 1 Machine Setup Day 2 Git & Github Day 3 Working with LLMs Day 4 Understanding the Agent Loop & Claude Code Day 5 Handling Context & MCP Servers

More weeks to come as the journey continues.

docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
Hey, I'm Francisco — a software engineering student working toward becoming a Full-Stack Developer.

I come from a background of curiosity and a desire to build things that matter. This blog is my attempt to capture the learning process honestly: the wins, the walls, and everything in between.

docs.title: The Program
docs.text:
I'm currently in an intensive full-stack development program. The curriculum covers:

  • Backend: Django & Django REST Framework
  • Database: PostgreSQL
  • Frontend: React + Vite
  • Tools: Git, GitHub, LLMs, Claude Code, MCP Servers

docs.title: Why This Blog
docs.text:
Writing about what I learn helps me retain it. If someone else stumbles across these posts and finds them useful, that's a bonus. But at its core, this is a record for me — proof that I showed up every day and tried to understand something new.

You can follow along week by week from the Home page.

docs.title: Day 1
docs.text:
Date: June 1, 2026

Title: Machine Setup — Getting the Tools in Place

Before you can write a single line of code, you have to make sure your machine is ready to run it. That was Day 1 in a nutshell.

We went through the full setup: installing the right versions of Python, Node, Git, and a handful of other tools that I'll be relying on throughout the program. We also configured our terminals, set up our editors, and made sure everything could actually talk to each other.

It sounds unglamorous, but there's something satisfying about getting a clean machine into a state where it's ready to do real work. Every tool installed felt like one less obstacle between me and actually building something.

The biggest takeaway: environments matter. The reason we set things up carefully is so that "it works on my machine" never becomes an excuse. A consistent, well-configured environment is the foundation everything else sits on.

Next: Day 2 — Git & Github

docs.title: Day 2
docs.text:
Date: June 2, 2026

Title: Git & Github — Version Control Is Non-Negotiable

Day 2 was all about Git and GitHub — the backbone of collaborative software development.

We covered the core concepts: repositories, commits, branches, merges, and pull requests. Git is one of those tools that looks simple on the surface but has real depth once you start working with teams and real codebases. Understanding the mental model — that Git tracks changes, not files — made a lot of things click.

GitHub added the social layer: forking repos, opening PRs, and understanding how open source collaboration actually works in practice.

The most important thing I walked away with: commit often, write meaningful messages, and branch early. A good Git workflow isn't just about saving your work — it's about communicating your intent to everyone else on the project (including future you).

Previous: Day 1 — Machine Setup | Next: Day 3 — Working with LLMs

docs.title: Day 3
docs.text:
Date: June 3, 2026

Title: Working with LLMs — A New Kind of Tool

Day 3 shifted gears entirely. Instead of infrastructure and tooling, we started exploring Large Language Models — what they are, how they work at a high level, and more importantly, how to work with them effectively as a developer.

LLMs are not magic, and they're not a replacement for understanding. What they are is an incredibly capable collaborator — one that responds to how you communicate with it. The quality of your output depends heavily on the quality of your input. Vague prompts get vague answers. Specific, well-structured prompts get useful ones.

We talked about the difference between using an LLM as a search engine (bad) versus using it as a thought partner or rubber duck (good). The goal is to stay in the driver's seat — using AI to accelerate your thinking, not outsource it.

The key insight: learn how to ask better questions. That skill transfers everywhere.

Previous: Day 2 — Git & Github | Next: Day 4 — The Agent Loop

docs.title: Day 4
docs.text:
Date: June 4, 2026

Title: The Agent Loop — How Claude Code Actually Works

Day 4 was one of the more mind-expanding days so far. We went under the hood to understand the agent loop — the cycle that powers tools like Claude Code.

At its core, an AI coding agent doesn't just respond to a single prompt. It operates in a loop: it reads context, decides on an action (like reading a file, running a command, or writing code), observes the result, and then decides what to do next. That loop repeats until the task is complete or it hits a dead end.

Understanding this changed how I think about interacting with these tools. When I give Claude Code a task, it's not executing one instruction — it's navigating a decision tree, using tools, and course-correcting in real time. That means the way I frame tasks, provide context, and set expectations actually matters a lot.

We also installed Claude Code itself and ran our first sessions. Seeing the loop play out in real time made the theory concrete.

The takeaway: an agent is only as good as the context it has. Your job as the human is to give it the right information and boundaries.

Previous: Day 3 — Working with LLMs | Next: Day 5 — MCP Servers

docs.title: Day 5
docs.text:
Date: June 5, 2026

Title: Handling Context & MCP Servers — Extending the Agent

The final day of week one tied everything together by going deeper on two related ideas: context management and MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers.

Context management is the practice of being intentional about what information you give an AI agent and when. Agents have a finite context window — they can only "see" so much at once. If you dump everything in, you get noise. If you're too sparse, the agent lacks what it needs. Learning to curate context is a skill, and one that directly affects the quality of what you get back.

MCP servers were the new concept of the day. They're a standardized way to connect external tools and data sources to an AI agent — essentially giving the agent new capabilities beyond its defaults. Think of it as a plugin system: you can wire up a database, a file system, an API, or any other resource, and the agent can call into it as part of its loop.

Together, context management and MCP servers are about giving the agent the right tools and information at the right time — which is really just good engineering practice applied to a new kind of system.

Week 1 done. On to building.
